strengths: Comprehensive and systematic study: The paper provides a clear and complete taxonomy of fairness guarantees (EF1, EFX, PROP1, MMS) across multiple information regimes (no information, normalization information, frequency predictions, and identical valuations).

Novel and elegant algorithmic contributions: Algorithm 1 introduces an intuitive outside-good certificate tracking mechanism that establishes PROP1 for any number of agents and EF1 for two agents under normalization. Even more significantly, Theorem 5.1 provides a general meta-algorithm lifting any offline share-based guarantee to the online setting under frequency predictions via picking sequences on identically ordered profiles.

Sharp and tight characterizations: The paper provides matching or tight bounds in several settings, notably showing that exactly $(\sqrt{5}-1)/2$-EFX is achievable and optimal for two agents with identical valuations under normalization information (Theorem 6.3), as well as strong zero-competitiveness impossibility results for EFX and EF1.

Learning-augmented analysis: The inclusion of models with noisy advice (both for normalization constants and frequency multisets) connects the theoretical online fair division framework nicely to the modern learning-augmented algorithms literature.

High clarity and scholarly rigor: The presentation is well-structured, mathematical proofs are rigorous and readable, and the manuscript corrects an erroneous impossibility construction from prior work (Kahana & Hazon, 2023).
weaknesses: Unresolved question for EF1 with frequency predictions: The achievable competitive ratio for EF1 when $n \ge 3$ under frequency predictions remains an open problem, though the authors explicitly and honestly acknowledge this conjecture.

Online instantiation error dependency: In the learning-augmented model with noisy frequency predictions (Section 5.1), the error $\eta_i$ depends on the chosen online instantiation rule rather than being bounded directly and purely in terms of an intrinsic metric (such as the 1-Wasserstein distance) between the true and predicted multisets.

strengths: Comprehensive and complete mapping: The paper provides a nearly complete taxonomy (summarized neatly in Table 1) characterizing the feasibility and impossibility of standard fairness axioms (EFX, EF1, PROP1, MMS) across three distinct information regimes: no information, normalization information, and frequency predictions.

Powerful meta-algorithm for frequency predictions: Theorem 5.1 demonstrates that any feasible share-based fairness guarantee from the offline setting can be seamlessly transferred to the online setting under adversarial arrival order using frequency predictions. This yields immediate state-of-the-art results, including (3/4 + 3/3836)-MMS for arbitrary n and exact EFX for n = 2.

Technically sound and tight bounds: The paper establishes matching impossibility results alongside positive guarantees, including tight bounds such as the exact golden ratio conjugate ((sqrt(5)-1)/2) for EFX under identical valuations with normalization.

Pragmatic learning-augmented analysis: The inclusion of robustness bounds against noisy normalization and noisy frequency predictions grounds the theoretical models nicely in realistic machine learning pipelines.

High presentation clarity: The manuscript is well-structured, easy to follow, and transparently details prior literature while correcting errors in past work (e.g., clarifying the invalid proof in Kahana & Hazon 2023).
weaknesses: Online multiset instantiation metric: In Theorem 5.7, the relative error epsilon_i depends on the specific online instantiation sequence rather than purely on an intrinsic distance between the true and predicted multisets (such as the 1-Wasserstein distance), leaving the optimal online matching strategy with provable distance bounds as an open question.

Open gap for EF1 with frequency predictions: While EFX is settled for n >= 3 (ruled out), the existence of an EF1 or alpha-EF1 allocation for n >= 3 under frequency predictions remains an unresolved open problem.

Strict ex-post adaptive adversarial model: The framework relies entirely on an adaptive adversary with deterministic/ex-post evaluation, which is quite strict and naturally drives strong impossibility results (e.g., Lemma A.1 showing randomization cannot bypass them). Exploring oblivious adversaries or ex-ante guarantees would offer valuable complementary insights.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic study: The paper provides a clear, unifying landscape (nicely summarized in Table 1) of what is achievable across different information models (no information, normalization information, frequency predictions) and valuation structures (general additive vs. identical) for key fair division notions (EF1, EFX, PROP1, MMS).

Strong technical contributions on positive results: Algorithm 1 introduces a novel outside-max certificate mechanism achieving PROP1 for all n and EF1 for n=2 under normalization information, resolving limitations of prior semi-online MMS algorithms. Furthermore, Theorem 5.1 provides a powerful meta-algorithm that lifts any feasible offline share-based guarantee directly to the online setting with frequency predictions via an identical-ordering reduction.

Tight bounds and clean impossibility constructions: Several tight or near-tight results are established, such as the exact golden ratio ((sqrt(5)-1)/2) bound for EFX with two agents under identical valuations and normalization (Theorem 6.3), as well as strong 0-competitiveness impossibility results for EF1/EFX under various advice regimes.

Conceptual rigor and scholarship: The paper clarifies and rectifies a known flaw in the literature (Kahana & Hazon, 2023) regarding PROP1 impossibilities, and appropriately extends lower bounds to randomized algorithms under the ex post adaptive adversarial model.
weaknesses: Unresolved open question for EF1 under frequency predictions: While the paper settles many cells in Table 1, the question of whether EF1 (or a positive approximation thereof) can be achieved for n >= 3 under frequency predictions remains open.

Formulation of the learning-augmented model for frequency predictions: In Section 5.1, the error parameter eta_i depends directly on the online instantiation rule rather than purely on the intrinsic distance between the predicted multiset and the realized multiset (e.g., Wasserstein distance); the authors acknowledge that bounding eta_i in terms of multiset distance remains an open problem.

Restricted adversary model leads to extreme impossibilities: By evaluating ex post guarantees against a fully adaptive adversary, many competitive ratios collapse strictly to 0 for n >= 3. While standard in worst-case analysis, exploring oblivious adversaries or ex ante/probabilistic relaxations would provide a more nuanced picture of intermediate fairness guarantees.

Absence of empirical evaluation: Although the paper is primarily theoretical, experimental simulations evaluating Algorithm 1 and the frequency-prediction heuristic on synthetic or real trace workloads (e.g., ad impressions or cloud tasks) would have strengthened the practical motivation.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and conceptually compelling topic at the intersection of fair division and online algorithms with advice/predictions, systematically categorizing fairness guarantees across several information regimes (no information, normalization, frequency predictions, and identical valuations).

The connection established in Section 5 between offline share-based fairness notions and online algorithms with frequency predictions via IDO (identical ordering) valuations and picking sequences (Theorem 5.1) is innovative and provides an interesting meta-algorithmic technique.
Theorem 6.3 establishes a tight bound of (sqrt(5)-1)/2 for EFX with two agents under identical valuations and normalization information, featuring a clean matching upper and lower bound construction.
The paper provides a helpful literature overview and correctly identifies an error in the previous literature (specifically in Kahana and Hazon, 2023).
weaknesses: The proof of Theorem 4.1 (Case 2, page 9) and Theorem 4.2 (page 10) contains a fundamental flaw. The author claims: 'For every inactive agent i in N \ N', we have that v_i(A_i) < 1/n (because if v_i(A_i) >= 1/n, then the agent i would have been added to the set of inactive agents before the last good was added to their bundle).' This assertion is mathematically false. In Algorithm 1, x_i is computed with a discounted weight (n-1)/n on the arriving good g (Line 7). Consequently, an agent can satisfy x_i < 1/n, be allocated g, and end up with bundle value v_i(A_i cup {g}) >= 1/n. In subsequent rounds, this agent becomes inactive while holding a bundle of value >= 1/n. Therefore, inactive agents can easily have v_i(A_i) >= 1/n, which invalidates the deduction that sum_{i in N} v_i(A_i) < 1, causing the contradiction arguments in both Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.2 to collapse.

Algorithm 1 has a severe runtime failure / pseudocode bug: Lines 3-5 check whether N' is empty at the beginning of the while loop, but all remaining active agents can satisfy x_i >= 1/n during Lines 6-11 within the current step. When this occurs, N' becomes empty, and Line 12 ('Let i in argmax_{j in N'} v_j(g)') attempts to choose an agent from an empty set, resulting in an undefined operation/crash.

The claim that N' = emptyset at termination in Theorem 4.1 is empirically disprovable on simple instances. For example, consider n=2 and four identical goods of value 0.25. Running Algorithm 1: g_1 goes to agent 1 (x_1 = 0.125, x_2 = 0.125); g_2 goes to agent 2 (x_1 = 0.375, x_2 = 0.125); g_3 goes to agent 1 (x_1 = 0.375, x_2 = 0.375); at g_4, agent 1 has x_1 = 0.5 + 0.5(0.25) = 0.625 >= 0.5 and becomes inactive, while agent 2 has x_2 = 0.25 + 0.125 = 0.375 < 0.5 and remains active. Good g_4 is allocated to agent 2, and the loop terminates with N' = {2} != emptyset. The contradiction argument claiming |N'| >= 1 is impossible is therefore unsound.

The proof of Proposition 3.1 (Case 1, page 7) is incorrect. The proof argues that if agents 1 and 2 each receive at least one good from {g_3, ..., g_{n+1}}, then some agent i in N \ {1, 2} receives no goods, 'leaving us with a 0-EF1 allocation, a contradiction.' However, in the constructed valuation profile on page 6, every agent i in N \ {1, 2} has valuation 0 for all goods in {g_3, ..., g_{n+1}}. For agent i, v_i(A_1 \ {g_1}) = 0 and v_i(A_2 \ {g_2}) = 0. Hence, v_i(A_i) = 0 >= v_i(A_j \ {g}) for all j, meaning agent i suffers zero envy up to one good (EF1 is satisfied for agent i). The allocation does not violate EF1, and no contradiction is reached.

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous theoretical landscape: The paper provides a systematic mapping of achievable and impossible fairness guarantees (EF1, EFX, PROP1, MMS, and general share-based fairness) across four distinct information models: no information, normalized valuations, frequency predictions, and identical valuations.

Strong positive result via Theorem 5.1: The meta-algorithm establishing that any feasible share-based fairness notion in the offline single-shot setting can be matched in the online setting given frequency predictions is conceptually elegant and broadly applicable (e.g., yielding online guarantees for (3/4 + 3/3836)-MMS).

Improvements and corrections to prior literature: The paper improves upon the results of Zhou et al. (ICML 2023) by showing how to achieve PROP1 for any n and EF1 for n = 2 under normalization, and corrects an existing error in the impossibility proof of Kahana & Hazon (2023).

Tight analysis in specialized regimes: Theorem 6.3 provides an exact, tight bound of (\sqrt{5}-1)/2-EFX for two agents with identical valuations and normalized sums, with matching upper and lower bounds.
Clarity and mathematical precision: The proofs are detailed, constructive, and clearly presented throughout the manuscript.
weaknesses: Strong prediction model without robustness analysis: The frequency prediction model assumes exact multiset knowledge of incoming valuation profiles. While motivated by online bin packing and knapsack literature, the manuscript does not analyze performance under noisy/perturbed predictions (consistency and robustness), which is standard in the broader learning-augmented algorithms literature.

Unresolved gap for EF1 under frequency predictions: The status of EF1 for n >= 3 with frequency predictions remains an open conjecture, leaving a slight gap in the otherwise complete characterization.

Structure and conference length constraints: The manuscript is currently written as a 24-page extended paper with all proofs inline. For standard conference proceedings, the main body must be condensed significantly into an 8–9 page format with non-essential proofs moved to an appendix.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic study: The paper provides a clear and unified picture of the boundaries of fairness (EF1, EFX, PROP1, MMS) across different information regimes (no information, normalization information, frequency predictions, and identical valuations).

Strong positive results: Theorem 5.1 provides an elegant and general meta-algorithm showing that any single-shot feasible share-based guarantee can be matched online given frequency predictions, directly unlocking the state-of-the-art (3/4 + 3/3836)-MMS bound in the online setting. Additionally, Algorithm 1 simultaneously guarantees PROP1 for all n and EF1 (as well as 0.5-MMS) for n=2 under normalized valuations.

Tight bounds and sharp characterizations: Theorem 6.3 establishes an exact, tight approximation ratio of (sqrt(5)-1)/2 for EFX in the case of two agents with identical valuations under normalization information, featuring matching upper and lower bounds.
Clear exposition and rigorous proofs: The mathematical proofs are detailed, sound, and clearly motivated with helpful connections to online scheduling and learning-augmented algorithms literature.
weaknesses: Perfect predictions assumption: The frequency predictions model assumes exact multiset valuations upfront. While this is an established information model in the online algorithms literature, the paper does not analyze robustness to prediction error (e.g., consistency vs. robustness tradeoffs as in learning-augmented algorithms).

Unresolved gap for EF1 under frequency predictions: The paper leaves open whether an EF1 allocation (or a positive approximation thereof) can be achieved for n >= 3 agents with frequency predictions, conjecturing impossibility without a proof.

Format and conference length: At 24 pages of main text (excluding references), the paper is structured more like a journal submission than a standard conference paper, and would need streamlining to fit standard page budgets.
